analysis.one_liner: Bans making, selling, or owning semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, with a federal buyback.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee with 3 cosponsors until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to knowingly import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon or a magazine holding more than 10 rounds. It lists hundreds of specific rifles, pistols, and shotguns by name, exempts traditional hunting and sporting firearms by name, carves out law enforcement and range use, and orders the ATF to run a buyback program to purchase and destroy the banned guns and magazines.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be communities exposed to mass shootings and gun violence, since the weapons the bill covers are the types most often used in those attacks. People who did not own the covered firearms would bear none of the transition cost.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon or a large-capacity ammunition feeding device, with the aim of removing them from circulation.

Orders the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives to run a buy-back program to purchase and destroy the banned weapons and magazines, compensating current owners rather than only punishing them.
Spares traditional hunting and sporting firearms: bolt, pump, lever, and slide-action guns, antiques, and hundreds of named hunting rifles and shotguns listed in an appendix are exempt.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of the covered firearms and magazines, who would have to sell them through the buyback or face criminal liability for possession, and the gun manufacturers and dealers whose best-selling product lines the bill covers. Federal taxpayers would fund the buyback.
analysis.who_pays_short: Current gun owners and the gun industry

drawbacks.text: The ban covers possession, not just future sales, so millions of Americans who already legally own the listed rifles, pistols, shotguns, and standard-capacity magazines would become subject to criminal penalty unless they turned them in through the buyback.

The definitions are feature-based, keyed to items like a pistol grip, threaded barrel, or barrel shroud on a semiautomatic rifle, so the ban sweeps in common firearms that function much like many exempted hunting guns; critics argue that punishes cosmetic features rather than demonstrated danger.

The bill includes hundreds of named exemptions for hunting and competition firearms in an appendix, a reminder that the line between banned and permitted semiautomatic guns is largely about looks and features, which invites the objection that it is arbitrary.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pursues a real public-safety goal with a tool that carries a heavy and broadly felt cost: a possession ban touching millions of lawful owners and the industry's core product line, softened somewhat by a buyback and sweeping exemptions for traditional hunting guns. Whether that trade is worth it is precisely the fight the bill never got to have; it died without any hearing or vote, so Congress never weighed the costs in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, and no one ever scheduled a hearing or markup, so it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-CA) introduced the bill on May 23, 2019.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, and on June 26, 2019 to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security.
No further action was ever taken; the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended.
Only three House Democrats cosponsored the bill out of 231 Democrats in the chamber, a sign of how little support it had even within the majority party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and sellers of the covered rifles, pistols, and magazines kept their market untouched, and current owners avoided any obligation to sell their firearms. Communities waiting for federal action on assault weapons got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Eric Swalwell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

for.name: 3 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other member joined.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee and its Crime Subcommittee leadership
against.role: Committee chairs with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the two-year Congress, leaving it to die in subcommittee.

against.name: National Rifle Association and allied gun-rights groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed assault-weapon bans of this kind and pressed members against them.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the party split was never tested; but the bill drew only 3 cosponsors out of 231 House Democrats and none from the Republican side, showing minimal support even within the majority party.

industries.industry: Semiautomatic rifle and pistol manufacturers (AR-15 and AK-style firearms)
industries.note: The bill's named list covers their flagship product lines, ending legal domestic sale and manufacture. Their interest in keeping those sales runs against the bill's public-safety purpose.
Dealers could no longer sell the banned weapons or magazines over 10 rounds, removing a major share of sales. Their interest in continued sales runs against the ban's purpose.

industries.industry: Traditional hunting and sporting firearms makers
industries.note: Hundreds of named bolt, lever, pump, and traditional semi-auto rifles and shotguns are exempted in Appendix A, leaving their product lines fully legal. Their exemption serves hunters and shooters whom the bill deliberately spared.
